title: The Day of the Dead
hook: in Mexico, All Souls is kept with altars, marigolds and photographs

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter baskets: eggs and bread under a white cloth, blessed on Holy Saturday. Your line was święconka. Did a shared meal get its pause? Day one thousand four hundred.

A table against the living room wall, covered in a bright cloth. On it, a framed photograph of a grandfather in a pressed shirt. Next to him, a glass of water, a candle, a plate of sweet bread dusted with sugar, a pack of the cigarettes he never quit, and a small bottle of the soda he liked. Orange marigolds everywhere, petals scattered in a path across the floor to the door. A crucifix or a picture of Our Lady of Guadalupe watches over it all. Later, the family will go to the cemetery to clean his grave, bring more flowers, and stay a while. In Mexico, this is one way families keep All Saints and All Souls. Today, the Day of the Dead.
screen: `A PHOTOGRAPH IN A PRESSED SHIRT.` → `MARIGOLDS IN A PATH TO THE DOOR.` → `STAYING A WHILE AT THE GRAVE.`

segments.voice: First, where it sits in the Church's year. The Church keeps the Solemnity of All Saints and, the next day, the Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed, All Souls. On All Souls, Catholics pray for everyone who has died. In Mexico, those two days became the Día de Muertos, the Day of the Dead, kept at home altars and in cemeteries as well as at Mass. Historians discuss how much of it also carries older Indigenous ways of honoring the dead. Second, the altar, the ofrenda, which means an offering. Photographs, so faces aren't forgotten. Favorite food and drink, because love remembers details. Candles, for light. Marigolds, whose color and scent, people say, help the dead find their way home. Those meanings are tradition, held with affection. Third, why a Catholic can keep it with joy. The book of Wisdom, in the Douay-Rheims: "But the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them." Catholics believe the dead are alive in God, and that the living can still pray for them. So the day isn't spooky, and it isn't a version of Halloween. It's a family reunion across the line of death, with the Church's prayers at its center. Last, look back at this week. A Mass for someone. An hour of hunger before communion. Fish and alms in Lent. A Jesse tree in Advent. Wise men crossing a living room. An Easter basket. Again and again, faith left the sanctuary for a kitchen, a table, a shelf. The Day of the Dead brings the whole family there too, the living and the dead.
screen: `ALL SAINTS, THEN ALL SOULS.` · `THE OFRENDA: PHOTOS, FOOD, LIGHT.` · `IN THE HAND OF GOD.` · `A WEEK OF FAITH AT HOME.` · then, large: `THE SOULS OF THE JUST ARE IN THE HAND OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set out a photo of someone who died. Settle, and breathe. Choose one person. If you have a picture nearby, on your phone or on a shelf, bring it in front of you. Look at their face. Remember one small thing they loved: a food, a song, a joke, a chair they always sat in. Let yourself smile if a smile comes. If you pray, you can ask God to give them eternal rest. If you don't, simply say their name and thank them for one thing. The bell holds the time.
The Day of the Dead. Día de Muertos: Mexico's way of keeping All Saints and All Souls, with home altars, marigolds, photographs and visits to the graves. Today's word.
screen: `THE DAY OF THE DEAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: they're remembered. Today, leave one photo of someone who has died where you'll pass it, and set something they loved beside it, even just a flower or a cup of coffee. Day one thousand four hundred.

howItsDone: In Mexico and among Mexican families elsewhere, Catholics keep All Saints and All Souls as the Día de Muertos: they build home altars with photographs, candles, marigolds and the favorite foods of those who have died, visit and decorate graves, and pray for the dead, often including Mass.
